title_zh: 三祖僧璨大師 信心銘
title_en: Inscription on Faith in Mind (Xinxin Ming)
author_zh: 三祖 僧璨 大師 (d. 606 CE)

stanzas.zh: 至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。但莫憎愛，洞然明白。
stanzas.pinyin: Zhì dào wú nán, wéi xián jiǎnzé. Dàn mò zēng ài, dòng rán míng bái.

suzuki.text: The Perfect Way knows no difficulties except that it refuses to make preferences; only when freed from hate and love, it reveals itself fully and without disguise.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The Great Way is not difficult, it only avoids picking and choosing. Just do not love or hate, and it is clearly evident.

red_pine.text: The Great Way is not hard, it only detests picking and choosing. Simply without hate or love, it opens wide and clear.

stanzas.zh: 毫釐有差，天地懸隔。欲得現前，莫存順逆。
stanzas.pinyin: Háo lí yǒu chà, tiān dì xuán gé. Yù dé xiàn qián, mò cún shùn nì.

suzuki.text: A tenth of an inch's difference, and heaven and earth are set apart; if you wish to see it before your own eyes, have no fixed thoughts either for or against it.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: If there is the slightest deviation, heaven and earth are set apart. If you want it to appear before you, do not harbor favorable or contrary thoughts.

red_pine.text: A hair's breadth of deviation, and heaven and earth are divided. If you want the Way to be present, have neither favorable nor adverse thoughts.

stanzas.zh: 違順相爭，是為心病。不識玄旨，徒勞念靜。
stanzas.pinyin: Wéi shùn xiāng zhēng, shì wéi xīn bìng. Bù shí xuán zhǐ, tú láo niàn jìng.

suzuki.text: To set up what you like against what you dislike—this is the disease of the mind; when the profound meaning of things is not understood, peace of mind is disturbed to no purpose.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: When favorable and adverse struggle, this is the mind's disease. Not recognizing the profound principle, one fruitlessly labors to quiet the thoughts.

red_pine.text: Conflict between liking and disliking is the disease of the mind. Without realizing the profound meaning, you struggle in vain to calm your thoughts.

stanzas.zh: 圓同太虛，無欠無餘。良由取捨，所以不如。
stanzas.pinyin: Yuán tóng tài xū, wú qiàn wú yú. Liáng yóu qǔ shě, suǒ yǐ bù rú.

suzuki.text: The Way is perfect like vast space where nothing is wanting and nothing is in excess; indeed, it is due to our choosing to accept or reject that we do not see the true nature of things.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Round like great emptiness, without lack or excess. It is due to accepting and rejecting that you do not see it as it is.

red_pine.text: All-embracing like great space, nothing is lacking, nothing left over. Because you grasp and reject, you are not in harmony.

stanzas.zh: 莫逐有緣，勿住空忍。一種平懷，泯然自尽。
stanzas.pinyin: Mò zhú yǒu yuán, wù zhù kōng rěn. Yī zhǒng píng huái, mǐn rán zì jìn.

suzuki.text: Live neither in the entanglements of outer things, nor in inner feelings of emptiness; be serene in the oneness of things and such erroneous views will disappear by themselves.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Do not pursue conditional existence, do not dwell in acceptance of emptiness. In a unified, even frame of mind, dualities naturally vanish.

red_pine.text: Do not chase after conditions, do not abide in empty endurance. In a single, tranquil mind, all errors naturally disappear.

stanzas.zh: 止動歸止，止更彌動。唯滯兩邊，寧知一種。
stanzas.pinyin: Zhǐ dòng guī zhǐ, zhǐ gèng mí dòng. Wéi zhì liǎng biān, nìng zhī yī zhǒng.

suzuki.text: When you strive to gain quiescence by stopping motion, the quiescence thus gained is ever in motion; as long as you tarry in the dualism, how can you realize oneness?

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Stopping activity to return to stillness, the stillness is even more active. As long as you remain caught in the extremes, how can you know the One?

red_pine.text: Stopping movement to find stillness only makes the stillness more restless. Lingering in either extreme, how can you know unity?

stanzas.zh: 一種不通，兩處失功。遣有沒有，從空背空。
stanzas.pinyin: Yī zhǒng bù tōng, liǎng chù shī gōng. Qiǎn yǒu méi yǒu, cóng kōng bèi kōng.

suzuki.text: And when oneness is not thoroughly understood, in two ways loss is sustained: the denying of reality is the asserting of it, and the asserting of emptiness is the denying of it.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: When the One is not mastered, both extremes lose their efficacy. Banishing existence is to lose existence; following emptiness is to turn your back on emptiness.

red_pine.text: If unity is not understood, effort is wasted in both directions. Denying reality asserts it; pursuing emptiness denies it.

stanzas.zh: 多言多慮，轉不相應。絕言絕慮，無處不通。
stanzas.pinyin: Duō yán duō lǜ, zhuǎn bù xiāng yìng. Jué yán jué lǜ, wú chù bù tōng.

suzuki.text: Wordiness and intellection—the more with them the further astray we go; away therefore with wordiness and intellection, and there is no place where we cannot pass freely.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The more words and thoughts, the further you wander from accord. Cut off words and thoughts, and there is nowhere you cannot penetrate.

red_pine.text: Too much talking and thinking only turn you away from harmony. Stop talking and thinking, and there is nowhere you cannot pass.

stanzas.zh: 歸根得旨，隨照失宗。須臾返照，勝卻前空。
stanzas.pinyin: Guī gēn dé zhǐ, suí zhào shī zōng. Xū yú fǎn zhào, shèng què qián kōng.

suzuki.text: When we return to the root, we gain the meaning; when we pursue the projection, we lose the source. At the moment of turning the light within, we transcend both emptiness and form.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Return to the root and you get the essence; follow appearances and you lose the source. One instant of inner illumination surpasses former emptiness.

red_pine.text: Returning to the root, you grasp the meaning; following appearances, you lose the essence. A moment of inward turning transcends any empty state.

stanzas.zh: 前空轉變，皆由妄見。不用求真，唯須息見。
stanzas.pinyin: Qián kōng zhuǎn biàn, jiē yóu wàng jiàn. Bù yòng qiú zhēn, wéi xū xī jiàn.

suzuki.text: The transformations going on in an empty world which confront us appear real all because of Ignorance; try not to seek after the true, only cease to cherish opinions.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The transformations of former emptiness are all due to deluded views. Do not try to seek truth, only cease to harbor views.

red_pine.text: All shifts in apparent emptiness arise from deluded perception. There is no need to seek truth, only cease holding opinions.

stanzas.zh: 二見不住，慎莫追尋。纔有是非，紛然失心。
stanzas.pinyin: Èr jiàn bù zhù, shèn mò zhuī xún. Cái yǒu shì fēi, fēn rán shī xīn.

suzuki.text: Abide not with dualism, carefully avoid pursuing it; as soon as you have right and wrong, confusion ensues, and Mind is lost.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Do not remain in dualistic views; take care not to pursue them. The moment there is right and wrong, the mind is lost in confusion.

red_pine.text: Do not abide in dualistic views, be careful not to seek them. As soon as right and wrong arise, the mind is lost in turmoil.

stanzas.zh: 二由一有，一亦莫守。一心不生，萬法無咎。
stanzas.pinyin: Èr yóu yī yǒu, yī yì mò shǒu. Yī xīn bù shēng, wàn fǎ wú jiù.

suzuki.text: The two exist because of the One, but hold not even to this One; when the one mind is not disturbed, the ten thousand things offer no offence.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Duality arises from the One; do not cling even to the One. When one mind does not arise, the ten thousand dharmas have no fault.

red_pine.text: The two arise from the One, but do not hold onto the One. When one mind does not stir, the ten thousand things are without blame.

stanzas.zh: 無咎無法，不生不心。能隨境滅，境逐能沉。
stanzas.pinyin: Wú jiù wú fǎ, bù shēng bù xīn. Néng suí jìng miè, jìng zhú néng chén.

suzuki.text: No offence is offered, and no ten thousand things; no mind is disturbed, and no mind is put to work. The subject is quieted when the object ceases, the object ceases when the subject is quieted.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: No fault, no dharma; no arising, no mind. The observer dissolves with the object; the object submerges with the observer.

red_pine.text: Without blame, without phenomena; without arising, without mind. The subject vanishes with the object; the object sinks with the subject.

stanzas.zh: 境由能境，能由境能。欲知兩段，元是一空。
stanzas.pinyin: Jìng yóu néng jìng, néng yóu jìng néng. Yù zhī liǎng duàn, yuán shì yī kōng.

suzuki.text: The object is an object for the subject, the subject is a subject for the object; know that the relativity of the two rests ultimately on the oneness of Emptiness.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Object is object because of the subject; subject is subject because of the object. If you want to know these two, originally they are one emptiness.

red_pine.text: An object exists because of the subject; the subject exists because of the object. If you wish to understand both, they are originally one emptiness.

stanzas.zh: 一空同兩，齊含萬象。不見精粗，寧有偏黨。
stanzas.pinyin: Yī kōng tóng liǎng, qí hán wàn xiàng. Bù jiàn jīng cū, nìng yǒu piān dǎng.

suzuki.text: In the oneness of Emptiness the two are one, and each of the two contains in itself all the ten thousand things; when no discrimination is made between this and that, how can a one-sided and prejudiced view arise?

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: One emptiness equals the two, equally containing the ten thousand images. Seeing no fine or coarse, how can there be taking sides?

red_pine.text: One emptiness unites the two, embracing all ten thousand forms alike. Seeing neither fine nor coarse, how could there be partiality?

stanzas.zh: 大道體寬，無易無難。小見狐疑，轉急轉遲。
stanzas.pinyin: Dà dào tǐ kuān, wú yì wú nán. Xiǎo jiàn hú yí, zhuǎn jí zhuǎn chí.

suzuki.text: The Great Way is calm and large-hearted, for it nothing is easy, nothing is hard; small views are irresolute, the more in haste the tardier they go.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The Great Way is broad in essence, neither easy nor difficult. Small views are full of doubt—the more you hurry, the slower you go.

red_pine.text: The Great Way is vast in substance, neither easy nor hard. Small minds harbor doubt; the more they rush, the slower they move.

stanzas.zh: 執之失度，必入邪路。放之自然，體無去住。
stanzas.pinyin: Zhí zhī shī dù, bì rù xié lù. Fàng zhī zì rán, tǐ wú qù zhù.

suzuki.text: Clinging is never kept within bounds, it is sure to go the wrong way; let go things as they are, and there is neither coming nor going.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Grasping loses the measure and certainly leads to wrong paths. Let it go naturally, and its essence neither comes nor goes.

red_pine.text: Clinging loses all measure and surely enters the wrong path. Letting go naturally, the substance neither comes nor stays.

stanzas.zh: 任性合道，逍遙絕惱。繫念乖真，昏沉不好。
stanzas.pinyin: Rèn xìng hé dào, xiāo yáo jué nǎo. Xì niàn guāi zhēn, hūn chén bù hǎo.

suzuki.text: Obey the nature of things, and you are in concord with the Way, calm and easy and free from annoyance; but when your thoughts are tied, you turn away from the truth, they grow heavier and duller and are not at all sound.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Follow your nature and accord with the Way, free and easy without vexation. Tying thoughts turns away from reality, sinking into dullness is not good.

red_pine.text: Trusting your nature accords with the Way, roaming free from affliction. Tying your thoughts violates the truth; sinking into stupor is poor practice.

stanzas.zh: 不好勞神，何用疏親。欲取一乘，勿惡六塵。
stanzas.pinyin: Bù hǎo láo shén, hé yòng shū qīn. Yù qǔ yī chéng, wù è liù chén.

suzuki.text: When they are not sound, the spirit is troubled; what is the use of being partial and one-sided then? If you want to walk the course of the One Vehicle, be not prejudiced against the six sense-objects.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Do not weary the spirit—what use are estrangement and intimacy? If you wish to take the One Vehicle, do not dislike the six sense fields.

red_pine.text: Why weary the spirit with liking and disliking, distance and intimacy? If you wish to ride the One Vehicle, do not reject the six sense objects.

stanzas.zh: 六塵不惡，還同正覺。智者無為，愚人自縛。
stanzas.pinyin: Liù chén bù è, hái tóng zhèng jué. Zhì zhě wú wéi, yú rén zì fù.

suzuki.text: When you are not prejudiced against the six sense-objects, you are then one with the Enlightenment; the wise are non-active, while the ignorant bind themselves up.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Not disliking the six sense fields is identical to true awakening. The wise practice non-action; fools bind themselves.

red_pine.text: Not rejecting the six senses is identical to perfect awakening. The wise abide in non-action; the foolish bind themselves.

stanzas.zh: 法無異法，妄自愛著。將心用心，豈非大錯。
stanzas.pinyin: Fǎ wú yì fǎ, wàng zì ài zhuó. Jiāng xīn yòng xīn, qǐ fēi dà cuò.

suzuki.text: While in the Dharma itself there is no individuation, they ignorantly attach themselves to particular objects. It is their own mind that creates illusions—is this not the greatest of all contradictions?

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: In the Dharma there are no separate dharmas, yet delusion loves and clings. Using mind to manipulate mind—is this not a great mistake?

red_pine.text: In truth there is no other Dharma; only delusion clings to preference. Using mind to apply mind—is this not a great mistake?

stanzas.zh: 迷生寂亂，悟無好惡。一切二邊，良由斟酌。
stanzas.pinyin: Mí shēng jì luàn, wù wú hǎo è. Yī qiè èr biān, liáng yóu zhēn zhuó.

suzuki.text: Ignorance begets the dualism of rest and unrest, the enlightened have no likes and dislikes: all forms of dualism are ignorantly contrived by the mind itself.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Delusion breeds stillness and disturbance; awakening has no likes and dislikes. All extremes of duality are born of calculation.

red_pine.text: Delusion creates stillness and agitation; awakening knows neither preference nor aversion. All dualistic extremes arise solely from deliberation.

stanzas.zh: 夢幻空華，何用把捉。得失是非，一時放卻。
stanzas.pinyin: Mèng huàn kōng huá, hé yòng bǎ zhuó. Dé shī shì fēi, yī shí fàng què.

suzuki.text: They are like unto visions and flowers in the air; why should we trouble ourselves to take hold of them? Gain and loss, right and wrong—away with them once for all!

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Dreams, illusions, flowers in the sky—why try to grasp them? Gain and loss, right and wrong—let go of them all at once.

red_pine.text: Dreams, phantoms, empty flowers—why try to grasp them? Gain and loss, right and wrong—release them all at once.

stanzas.zh: 眼若不寐，諸夢自除。心若不異，萬法一如。
stanzas.pinyin: Yǎn ruò bù mèi, zhū mèng zì chú. Xīn ruò bù yì, wàn fǎ yī rú.

suzuki.text: If an eye never falls asleep, all dreams will by themselves cease: if the Mind retains its absoluteless, the ten thousand things are of one Suchness.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: If the eye does not sleep, all dreams vanish by themselves. If the mind does not discriminate, the ten thousand dharmas are of one suchness.

red_pine.text: If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams naturally vanish. If the mind does not discriminate, the ten thousand things are one suchness.

stanzas.zh: 一如體玄，兀爾忘緣。萬法齊觀，歸復自然。
stanzas.pinyin: Yī rú tǐ xuán, wù ěr wàng yuán. Wàn fǎ qí guān, guī fù zì rán.

suzuki.text: When the deep mystery of one Suchness is fathomed, all of a sudden we forget the external entanglements; when the ten thousand things are viewed in their oneness, we return to the origin and remain where we ever have been.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The essence of one suchness is profound; unmoved, you forget conditions. Viewing the ten thousand dharmas equally, you return to the natural state.

red_pine.text: The substance of one suchness is deep and mysterious; resting still, conditions are forgotten. Beholding all things equally, you return to spontaneity.

stanzas.zh: 泯其所以，不可方比。止動無動，動止無止。
stanzas.pinyin: Mǐn qí suǒ yǐ, bù kě fāng bǐ. Zhǐ dòng wú dòng, dòng zhǐ wú zhǐ.

suzuki.text: Forget the wherefore of things, and we attain to a state beyond analogy: movement stopped is no movement, and rest set in motion is no rest.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Obliterate the whys and wherefores, and it cannot be compared. Rest in motion is no motion; motion in rest is no rest.

red_pine.text: Erasing all whys and wherefores, it cannot be compared. Stillness in motion is not motion; motion in stillness is not stillness.

stanzas.zh: 兩既不成，一何有爾。究竟窮極，不存軌則。
stanzas.pinyin: Liǎng jì bù chéng, yī hé yǒu ěr. Jiū jìng qióng jí, bù cún guǐ zé.

suzuki.text: When dualism does no more obtain, even oneness itself remains not as such. The ultimate end of things where they cannot go any further is not bound by rules and measures.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: When two are not established, how can One exist? At the ultimate limit, no rules or standards remain.

red_pine.text: When the two are not formed, how can one exist? At the ultimate limit, no rules or models apply.

stanzas.zh: 契心平等，所作俱息。狐疑盡淨，正信調直。
stanzas.pinyin: Qì xīn píng děng, suǒ zuò jū xī. Hú yí jìn jìng, zhèng xìn tiáo zhí.

suzuki.text: In the Mind harmonious with the Way we have the principle of identity, in which we find all strivings quieted; doubts and irresolutions are completely done away with, and the right faith is restored.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: In a mind attuned to equality, all striving ceases. Suspicion and doubt are cleansed; right faith is straightforward.

red_pine.text: In a mind of equality, all striving comes to rest. Doubts are thoroughly washed away, and true faith is upright.

stanzas.zh: 一切不留，無可記憶。寂然虛明，不勞心力。
stanzas.pinyin: Yī qiè bù liú, wú kě jì yì. Jì rán xū míng, bù láo xīn lì.

suzuki.text: Nothing is left behind, there is nothing to remember; all is void, lucid, and self-illuminating; there is neither stain, nor exertion, nor wasting of energy.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Nothing lingers, nothing to remember. Serene, empty, and bright, without toiling mental effort.

red_pine.text: Nothing is retained, nothing to remember. Still, empty, and bright, without exerting the mind.

stanzas.zh: 非思量處，識情難測。真如法界，無他無自。
stanzas.pinyin: Fēi sī liáng chù, shì qíng nán cè. Zhēn rú fǎ jiè, wú tā wú zì.

suzuki.text: This is where thinking never attains, this is where the imagination fails to measure. In the higher realm of True Suchness there is neither 'self' nor 'other'.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: A place beyond deliberation, difficult for intellect to measure. In the Dharma realm of true suchness, there is no other, no self.

red_pine.text: Where deliberation cannot reach, difficult for consciousness to measure. In the Dharma realm of true suchness, there is neither self nor other.

stanzas.zh: 要急相應，唯言不二。不二皆同，無不包容。
stanzas.pinyin: Yào jí xiāng yìng, wéi yán bù èr. Bù èr jiē tóng, wú bù bāo róng.

suzuki.text: When direct identification is sought, we can only say, 'Not two.' In being not two all is the same, all that exists is comprehended in it.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: To accord directly, only say 'not two.' In not two, all is identical, encompassing everything.

red_pine.text: To harmonize immediately, simply speak of non-duality. In non-duality all is equal, leaving nothing unencompassed.

stanzas.zh: 十方智者，皆入此宗。宗非促延，一念萬年。
stanzas.pinyin: Shí fāng zhì zhě, jiē rù cǐ zōng. Zōng fēi cù yán, yī niàn wàn nián.

suzuki.text: The wise in the ten quarters, they all enter into this absolute Faith. This absolute Faith is beyond quickening or extending, one instant is ten thousand years.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The wise of the ten directions all enter this essence. The essence is neither brief nor prolonged—one thought is ten thousand years.

red_pine.text: The wise of the ten directions all enter this teaching. The teaching is neither fast nor slow; one thought is ten thousand years.

stanzas.zh: 無在不在，十方目前。極小同大，忘絕境界。
stanzas.pinyin: Wú zài bù zài, shí fāng mù qián. Jí xiǎo tóng dà, wàng jué jìng jiè.

suzuki.text: There is no here, no there, but everywhere the whole ten quarters are immediately before us. The infinitely small is as large as the infinitely great, for limits and boundaries are forgotten.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: Whether present or not present, the ten directions are right before your eyes. The smallest is like the largest, bounds and limits forgotten.

red_pine.text: Neither present nor absent, the ten directions are right before your eyes. The infinitely small equals the great, bounds and limits forgotten.

stanzas.zh: 極大同小，不見邊表。有即是無，無即是有。
stanzas.pinyin: Jí dà tóng xiǎo, bù jiàn biān biǎo. Yǒu jí shì wú, wú jí shì yǒu.

suzuki.text: The infinitely large is as small as the infinitely small, for limits and boundaries are invisible. What is is what is not, what is not is what is.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The largest is like the smallest, no edges or surfaces seen. What is is what is not; what is not is what is.

red_pine.text: The infinitely great equals the small, no borders or surfaces seen. Existence is non-existence; non-existence is existence.

stanzas.zh: 若不如此，必不須守。一即一切，一切即一。
stanzas.pinyin: Ruò bù rú cǐ, bì bù xū shǒu. Yī jí yī qiè, yī qiè jí yī.

suzuki.text: Where things are not as this, you should never hold onto them. One is all, all is one.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: If it is not like this, surely you must not hold to it. One is all, all is one.

red_pine.text: If it is not like this, surely do not cling to it. One is all, all is one.

stanzas.zh: 但能如是，何慮不畢。信心不二，不二信心。
stanzas.pinyin: Dàn néng rú shì, hé lǜ bù bì. Xìnxīn bù èr, bù èr xìnxīn.

suzuki.text: When you realize this, what need is there to worry about not being complete? Faith in Mind is non-duality; non-duality is Faith in Mind.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: If you can be like this, why worry about completion? Faith in mind is not two; not two is faith in mind.

red_pine.text: Simply being like this, why worry about unfinished work? Faith in mind is not two; not two is faith in mind.

stanzas.zh: 言語道斷，非去來今。
stanzas.pinyin: Yányǔ dào duàn, fēi qù lái jīn.

suzuki.text: The way of words is cut off; there is no past, future, or present.

source.edition: D.T. Suzuki, The Eastern Buddhist Society (Kyoto), 1935 — Section IV.2 'On Believing in Mind (Shinjin-no-mei)'
source.verification: Public-domain text transcribed from sacred-texts.com (scan 2000) and the Golden Elixir Press 2015 PD reprint; stanza wording matches verbatim.

cleary.text: The way of words is cut off, neither past, future, nor present.

red_pine.text: The path of words is cut off; there is neither past, future, nor present.
